source_text: Ac per hoc, ut peccatum motui libero, ita naturam Deo abscribimus conditori. Est igitur natura humana bonum opus Dei; est libertas arbitrii, id est, possibilitas vel delinquendi, vel recte faciendi, bonum aeque opus Dei. Utrumque hoc homini a necessario venit; neutra de his duabus rebus mali causa est. Sed huc usque necessaria illa venerunt; iam voluntas quidem in his exoritur, sed non de his. Capacia voluntatis sunt quippe, non plena; nec faciunt, sed accipiunt diversitatem meritorum.
pass_a_gloss: And through this, as we ascribe sin to a free motion, so nature to God the founder. Human nature is therefore a good work of God; there is freedom of decision, that is, a possibility either of offending or of doing rightly, equally a good work of God. Each of these came to the human from the necessary; neither of these two things is a cause of evil. But thus far those necessary things came; now will indeed arises in these, but not from these. For they are capable of will, not full; nor do they make, but they receive a diversity of deserts.

lemmas.lexica: LS necessitas; Blaise vs free choice
LS voluntas=will, wish; Blaise moral will
LS arbitrium=judgment, free decision; Blaise liberum arbitrium
LS peccatum=fault, error; Blaise Christian sin
LS/Blaise natura=created constitution, not 'original sin' itself
LS conditor; Blaise God as maker from nothing
LS meritum; Blaise; glossary: desert not treasury-of-merit
LS malum; Blaise malum naturale vs malum voluntatis

pass_b_english: Consequently, just as we assign sin to a free movement, so we assign nature to God the creator. Human nature is therefore God’s good work. Freedom of will—that is, the possibility either of wrongdoing or of acting rightly—is equally God’s good work. Both come to the human being from necessity; neither is the cause of evil. But those necessary things extend only this far. Will now arises within them, but not from them. They possess the capacity for will, but are not filled with it. They do not produce but receive the differences in moral desert.

choices.why: Glossary default: arbitrium is the decision-power, not a later Augustinian/Reformation free-will locus.
Julian's definition of sin is an act of will. Keep 'will' rather than later 'free will' system language unless liberum arbitrium is present.
Julian's charge against Augustine: treating evil as a nature rather than as will.

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded.

speaker: Julian of Eclanum (words preserved in Augustine, Opus imperfectum contra Iulianum); Augustine's reply at this locus is excluded.
